item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
My initial interpretation was that the object was showing them fraudulent images after they tried to "game" it by having multiple people in one "session". I based this on the way both researchers calmed down after seeing the second photo of Dr. █████'s daughter - like, they both knew it hadn't happened to _them,_ so they'd believe the other guy hadn't either. It also seemed highly dubious that a researcher who knew they had something like that in their past would consent to testing a skip that generates photos of important, defining moments in their lives.

I'm no longer very confident about this interpretation. I don't find it particularly hard to believe that a scientist brilliant enough to work at the Foundation could pass any psych test they wanted to, and background checks don't tend to turn this kind of thing up unless the person under scrutiny actually got hauled in by the cops over it.

Super gross, and super disappointing in the researchers. But it doesn't seem far-fetched.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
Those tests could use a solid rewrite, really. Testing on doctors seems like a huge issue alone but my problem is the randomness. As if someone found the envelopes, worked out the basics and then, instead of trying to really test out the limits of those things, went like… "let's just throw a bunch of random dudes just to fill in the experiment log". The first and the last are the only justifiable tests in this skip.

And why, in the second test, the fourth photo comes out blank? Did the 3 previous photos took ALL of the doctor's memories? Or does it target only specific memories? Well, we don't know because no one thought about testing that. Bah, even if it did target specific memories, why stop at 3? Did she remember only 3 events from her relationship?

This whole article feels generally underplanned and underthought.

item.title: Tone
item.content:encoded:
The concept is good, it's just the writing seems to be a bit spotty. "Crystal clear" isn't scientific; "clear" would have sufficed. And conciseness is key as well: "use" means exactly the same as "utilize" and is two syllables, four letters shorter.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
The concept is fairly interesting, and even creepy, but some of the shenanigans in the tests seem a tad prurient and just there for titillation and whatnot. (Oooo, look at the pervert doctors!) The ghost one just seems… well, it's either pointless, or it wasn't properly expounded upon as to whether this thing is capable of producing images of memories or imaginings and fantasies as well. Plus randomly selecting from actual staff such as the doctors to do tests that wipe out their memories seems a little extreme even for the Foundation… they normally use the D-class for the permanently altering stuff unless the doctors and agents volunteer, that's what they're there for. You're already sacrificing a lot for the Foundation, and then they randomly pick you to have a memory of your kindly old grandpa wiped out for a test that they could have done selecting at random among the D-class? I hope she at least got a bonus in her next paycheck.

I'd take out the test with the pervert doctors and replace it with a test on a D-class who was either naturally amnesiac or had been given sufficient amnesiacs to wipe out his prior memories completely. He might just draw blank photos and it thus wouldn't be as interesting as other tests, but it has a reasonable purpose as opposed to "lol let's see what happens lol".

item.content:encoded: Ok, thing is, I don't think that the SCP foundation is really competitive. There are good SCPs, and terrible SCPs. Outside of that though, no SCP is really 'better' than another. if ten people like and upvote one, and eight people upvote another, then two people downvote.. Does it really matter? item.title: Fishmonger's vote
item.content:encoded:
Because it matters to me, I wanted to note here that Fishmonger's did not apparently come from the quality of the work but rather from IRC shenanigans because they did not like me asking people who had previously voted the old SCP-404 to re-read and re-vote if they thought it deserved it.

Call me crazy but I'm of the opinion that ratings on a page should immediately reflect whether or not you liked the CONTENT and not the results of backroom behavior. The ratings matter to me because I can look at who liked what, who didn't like what, rethink issues, and re-write them if necessary.

I know it's fairly BAWWWWish to be bothered by something like this but immature rating shit should really be avoided. If you like it, up-vote it, if you don't, down-vote it, but try to give some kind of constructive reference as to why instead of 'DURRRRRR I DON'T LIKE U'. Some of us actually do CARE to know that the things we write are held in a positive or negative light and try to use that input as a basis on whether to continue writing things or stop and look at current writings to see what can be improved. Maybe not everyone does that, but I do. More-so since I'm trying to breathe life into already down-rated SCPs, unfounded votes don't help me properly gauge if it's working or not.

So, yeah, that down vote apparently came from that. Thank you to the people who voted because you liked or disliked it.

Edit: One of the votes was removed so I edited my rant to reflect that. The sentiment 'Rate the work' still applies.

That assumes that:

  1. The newspaper was made on Earth.
  2. No more nuclear explosions takes place on Earth for the next few centuries.

Those are awfully big assumptions given the nature of this newspaper and the kind of world the Foundation lives in. Remember, a lot of Foundation sites have nuclear warheads set to go off in an emergency.

item.title: Re:
item.content:encoded:
Perhaps the use of chlorine-36 instead of the more common carbon-14 would be a better scientific dating method in this case. Chlorine-36 was produced in nuclear testing and therefore we know when a majority of it was dumped into the environment.

Supposing that no new nuclear explosions occur the dating could be made using standard half life calculations e.g. less carbon-36 than current norms but more than what was available pre-nuclear testing.

Just a quick thought on the matter of radiometric dating of objects from the future
